source.title: Building the Treasury
source.summary: Synthesizing the series: what an Islamic fiscal framework would look like in practice, what's missing, and what's next.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: The final episode brings together the building blocks: revenue (zakat, kharaj, resource-sharing), spending (the dual bayt al-mal and waqf model), borrowing (sukuk and revenue-backed instruments), and governance (fiscal transparency, accountability, the ruler as trustee). What would a coherent Islamic fiscal framework look like in a modern state? The honest answer: it would combine Islamic tax instruments with pragmatic additional revenue sources, because zakat alone cannot fund a modern welfare state. The framework would emphasize asset-backed borrowing over interest-bearing debt, dual provision over pure state monopoly, and institutional accountability over discretionary spending. No Muslim-majority country has fully implemented this, but partial experiments in Malaysia, the Gulf, and elsewhere offer real data. Islamic fiscal theory is a work in progress, and this episode says so plainly.

thread: Medieval Islamic rulers used zakat, kharaj, and waqf institutions. Modern Muslim states use income tax, bonds, and central budgets. We kept the names but borrowed the Westminster system.
The honest truth: zakat alone cannot fund a modern welfare state. Islamic fiscal theory meets reality when you need roads, hospitals, and defense budgets.
So the real framework combines Islamic instruments with pragmatic additions. Asset-backed sukuk instead of interest bonds. Dual provision through both state and waqf.

No Muslim-majority country has fully implemented this hybrid model. But Malaysia and the Gulf states have started testing pieces of what could become something entirely new. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-trt-6
